questions.question: What percentage of engineer time is typically spent working with production systems according to industry research?
options: 50% of their time
60% of their time
70% of their time
80% of their time
questions.explanation: Engineers typically spend 70% of their time working with production systems - incidents, optimization, customer issues, and maintenance.

questions.question: Which metric represents the time between when an incident is detected and when it's fully resolved?
options: MTTD (Mean Time To Detect)
MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures)
MTTR (Mean Time To Resolve)
MTTA (Mean Time To Acknowledge)
questions.explanation: MTTR (Mean Time To Resolve) measures the entire lifecycle from detection to resolution of an incident.

questions.question: What does an AI agent do when investigating production issues?
options: Only generates reports for humans to read
Formulates hypotheses, gathers evidence, and provides recommendations
Replaces all human engineers completely
Only monitors logs without taking action
questions.explanation: AI agents autonomously investigate by forming hypotheses across domains, collecting evidence, and providing actionable recommendations.

questions.question: During a production incident, what's the first critical step?
options: Writing a detailed postmortem report
Identifying and restoring service
Scheduling a team meeting
Updating documentation
questions.explanation: The priority during incidents is always to restore service first, then investigate root cause and prevent recurrence.

questions.question: What are the three main domains that production systems span?
options: Frontend, backend, and database
Development, staging, and production
Code, infrastructure, and telemetry
People, process, and technology
questions.explanation: Modern production systems require understanding across code, infrastructure, and telemetry to effectively operate and troubleshoot.

questions.question: What is 'toil' in the context of engineering work?
options: Complex algorithmic challenges
Manual, repetitive work that doesn't scale
Writing new features for customers
Learning new programming languages
questions.explanation: Toil refers to manual, repetitive, automatable work that grows with service size and doesn't provide lasting value.

questions.question: What type of data helps you understand the internal state of a running system?
options: Marketing analytics
Source code comments
Observability data (logs, metrics, traces)
User feedback surveys
questions.explanation: Observability data - logs, metrics, and traces - provides visibility into the internal behavior and health of production systems.

questions.question: What's a common challenge when optimizing cloud infrastructure costs?
options: Cloud services are always optimally priced by default
Identifying unused resources and rightsizing based on actual usage
Cloud costs never increase over time
All resources are equally important to keep
questions.explanation: Cost optimization requires continuously identifying waste, unused resources, and opportunities to rightsize based on actual usage patterns.

questions.question: What advantage does multi-agent orchestration provide over single AI responses?
options: It's faster because multiple agents work simultaneously
Deep investigation with specialized agents gathering evidence across domains
It uses less computational resources
It requires no training or configuration
questions.explanation: Multi-agent systems enable deep investigation where specialized agents work together to gather evidence and form comprehensive solutions.

questions.question: Why is cross-domain expertise valuable in production systems?
options: It makes engineers work longer hours
Issues span code, infrastructure, and telemetry - requiring connection across all three
It's only useful for senior executives
It eliminates the need for documentation
questions.explanation: Production issues rarely exist in isolation - they require understanding how code, infrastructure, and telemetry interact.

questions.question: What does SRE stand for in software engineering?
options: Software Reliability Engineering
Site Reliability Engineering
System Recovery Engineering
Service Resolution Engineering
questions.explanation: SRE (Site Reliability Engineering) is a discipline that applies software engineering approaches to infrastructure and operations.

questions.question: What is a 'root cause' in incident management?
options: The first person who reported the issue
The underlying reason that caused the incident
The symptom that users experienced
The time when the incident started
questions.explanation: Root cause is the fundamental reason an incident occurred - fixing it prevents the same issue from recurring.

questions.question: What's the benefit of having AI understand your existing production architecture?
options: It requires rebuilding everything from scratch
Provides recommendations that work with your current systems
It makes all legacy systems obsolete
It only works with brand new applications
questions.explanation: AI that understands existing architecture can provide practical recommendations that integrate with current systems rather than requiring rewrites.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the three pillars of observability?
options: Logs
Metrics
Screenshots
Traces
questions.explanation: The three pillars of observability are logs, metrics, and traces - screenshots are not a standard observability signal.

questions.question: What does it mean for AI to 'execute' in production systems?
options: It only suggests what humans should do
It operates tools, runs queries, and takes action autonomously
It deletes all production data
It only writes documentation
questions.explanation: Expert execution means AI can operate tools like an engineer - running queries, validating results, and adjusting approaches.

questions.question: Why do production systems constantly change?
options: Because engineers like to break things
New code deploys, infrastructure updates, and tooling evolves across teams
They don't change - production is always stable
Only during major migrations
questions.explanation: Production systems are dynamic - continuous deployments, infrastructure changes, and tooling updates happen across many teams.

questions.question: What's the goal of continuous integration and deployment (CI/CD)?
options: To prevent any code changes from happening
To automate building, testing, and deploying code frequently
To make deployments happen only once per year
To eliminate the need for testing
questions.explanation: CI/CD automates the software delivery process, enabling teams to release changes frequently and reliably.

questions.question: What's a common source of wasted cloud spending?
options: Using cloud services at all
Resources running 24/7 that are only needed during business hours
Having any redundancy for reliability
Using managed services
questions.explanation: Many organizations waste money on always-on resources that could be scheduled or rightsized based on actual usage patterns.

questions.question: What should happen after resolving a major production incident?
options: Immediately forget about it and move on
Conduct a blameless postmortem to learn and prevent recurrence
Fire whoever was on-call
Delete all logs to save space
questions.explanation: Blameless postmortems help teams learn from incidents and implement systemic improvements without assigning blame.

questions.question: What makes senior engineers particularly valuable during incidents?
options: They work longer hours than junior engineers
Cross-domain expertise connecting code, infrastructure, and telemetry
They have access to secret documentation
They never make mistakes
questions.explanation: Senior engineers excel at connecting dots across domains - understanding how code, infrastructure, and observability data interact.

questions.question: What's the primary difference between monitoring and observability?
options: Monitoring tracks known problems; observability helps understand unknown issues
They are exactly the same thing with different names
Observability is cheaper than monitoring
Monitoring is only for cloud systems
questions.explanation: Monitoring tracks predefined metrics for known issues. Observability provides insights to investigate and understand unknown problems.

questions.question: In a microservices architecture, what makes root cause analysis challenging?
options: Issues cascade across multiple services with complex dependencies
There are too few services to track
All services are perfectly isolated
Microservices never have incidents
questions.explanation: Microservices create complex dependency chains where issues in one service can cascade and manifest differently across many services.

questions.question: How does an AI agent differ from traditional automation scripts?
options: Agents adapt and learn; scripts follow fixed rules
Scripts are always faster than agents
Agents only work offline
Scripts can handle any unexpected scenario
questions.explanation: AI agents can adapt to new situations and learn from context, while traditional scripts execute predetermined steps.

questions.question: What does 'context switching' cost engineering teams during incidents?
options: Extra licensing fees for monitoring tools
Time and cognitive load moving between tools and gathering context
Physical server switching hardware
Network bandwidth
questions.explanation: Engineers lose significant time and mental capacity switching between tools, correlating data, and building mental models during investigations.

questions.question: What challenge do distributed traces help solve?
options: Reducing cloud costs
Understanding request flow across multiple services
Writing better code comments
Managing user authentication
questions.explanation: Distributed traces track requests across service boundaries, making it possible to understand latency and failures in complex systems.

questions.question: Why is institutional knowledge important in production systems?
options: It helps new engineers avoid repeating past mistakes and investigations
It's only useful for legal compliance
It increases the time to resolve incidents
It makes documentation unnecessary
questions.explanation: Institutional knowledge captures learnings from past incidents, patterns, and solutions that accelerate future troubleshooting.

questions.question: What's the challenge with optimizing observability tool costs?
options: Balancing data retention needs against exponentially growing ingestion costs
Observability tools are always free
More data always leads to better outcomes
There's no cost associated with telemetry
questions.explanation: Observability costs scale with data volume - teams must balance comprehensive visibility against budget constraints.

questions.question: What makes troubleshooting Kubernetes issues complex?
options: Kubernetes never has any issues
It only requires knowing one technology
Multiple abstraction layers (pods, nodes, services, ingress) interact dynamically
All issues are clearly documented
questions.explanation: Kubernetes complexity comes from multiple abstraction layers that interact - pods, deployments, services, networking, and storage.

questions.question: What's the risk of adding new features to a complex production system?
options: Features always work perfectly on first try
Unintended interactions with existing code, infrastructure, or data flow
New features reduce system complexity
There's no risk if you're careful
questions.explanation: In complex systems, new features can interact unexpectedly with existing components, causing cascading issues.

questions.question: What's the primary goal of reducing on-call burden?
options: Eliminating on-call rotations completely
Reducing alert noise and automating responses to known issues
Making incidents happen only during business hours
Ensuring alerts never fire
questions.explanation: The goal is meaningful on-call with fewer false alarms and automated handling of routine issues, not elimination of on-call.

questions.question: What makes hypothesis formation important in automated incident response?
options: Hypotheses are only for academic research
It enables systematic investigation of potential causes rather than random checking
Hypotheses slow down incident response
Only humans can form useful hypotheses
questions.explanation: Hypothesis-driven investigation focuses effort on likely causes and ensures systematic coverage of possibilities.

questions.question: When building on existing production systems, what's the key challenge?
options: Old systems should always be completely replaced
Understanding current architecture constraints and integration points
New features never affect old systems
Documentation is always up-to-date and complete
questions.explanation: Extending existing systems requires deep understanding of current architecture, constraints, and how new components will integrate.

questions.question: What's a canary deployment strategy?
options: Deploying to all servers at once for speed
Rolling out changes to a small subset first to detect issues early
Never deploying on Fridays
Requiring manager approval for every deploy
questions.explanation: Canary deployments release changes to a small percentage of traffic first, enabling quick rollback if issues are detected.

questions.question: What's the '80/20' problem in production data analysis?
options: 80% of your data is useless
Engineers spend 80% of time finding and preparing data, 20% analyzing it
20% of engineers do 80% of the work
80% of incidents happen on 20% of services
questions.explanation: Most analysis time is spent on data discovery, extraction, and preparation rather than actual insight generation.

questions.question: Why is production access control complex?
options: Engineers need broad access for incidents but minimal access for security
Everyone should have full production access always
Security doesn't matter in production
Access control is simple and straightforward
questions.explanation: Organizations must balance rapid incident response (needs broad access) with security best practices (minimal access).

questions.question: What's 'alert fatigue' and why is it harmful?
options: Feeling tired after exercising
Engineers ignore alerts due to excessive false positives and noise
Alerts that trigger too slowly
Having too few alerts
questions.explanation: Alert fatigue occurs when excessive false alarms cause engineers to ignore or dismiss notifications, missing real issues.

questions.question: What makes database performance issues particularly challenging?
options: Databases never have performance issues
Symptoms appear in applications but root cause is in query patterns or data modeling
Database issues are always obvious
Performance problems fix themselves
questions.explanation: Database performance issues manifest downstream in applications, requiring correlation between app behavior and database internals.

questions.question: What's 'cloud sprawl' and why does it matter?
options: When cloud data centers expand physically
Uncontrolled proliferation of resources across accounts and regions
The natural growth of business
A type of cloud storage
questions.explanation: Cloud sprawl is uncontrolled resource creation that leads to waste, security gaps, and management complexity.

questions.question: Why do organizations implement change freezes before major events?
options: Changes always cause outages
To reduce risk of incidents during critical business periods
Engineers need vacations
Change freezes eliminate all risk
questions.explanation: Change freezes minimize disruption risk during critical periods (holidays, sales events) by limiting production modifications.

questions.question: What's the limitation of pre-production testing for production issues?
options: Testing is completely unnecessary
Production has scale, data, and traffic patterns impossible to replicate
Test environments are always identical to production
All bugs can be found in staging
questions.explanation: Production scale, real user behavior, and data characteristics often reveal issues that don't appear in test environments.

questions.question: Why does production documentation often become outdated?
options: Engineers intentionally sabotage documentation
Systems evolve faster than documentation updates
Documentation tools are too expensive
No one knows how to write documentation
questions.explanation: Production systems change continuously through deployments and updates, while documentation updates lag behind operational changes.

questions.question: What makes capacity planning challenging in modern systems?
options: Capacity planning is always perfectly accurate
Unpredictable traffic patterns and complex resource interdependencies
Infrastructure never has capacity constraints
Planning is only done once per decade
questions.explanation: Modern systems face variable traffic, complex dependencies, and dynamic resource needs that make capacity forecasting difficult.

questions.question: What's an SLO (Service Level Objective)?
options: A target reliability metric the service commits to
A legal contract with customers
The maximum speed code can execute
A database query optimization
questions.explanation: SLOs define target reliability levels (like 99.9% uptime) that services aim to maintain for users.

questions.question: What's a common cause of 'intermittent' production issues?
options: Intermittent issues don't actually exist
Load-dependent behavior or race conditions under specific conditions
Engineers imagining problems
Intermittent issues are always DNS
questions.explanation: Intermittent issues often result from load-dependent behavior, race conditions, or edge cases that occur under specific conditions.

questions.question: What does 'production parity' mean in development?
options: Dev and production should have identical configurations and dependencies
Production and development are completely different
Only senior engineers access production
Development environments don't matter
questions.explanation: Production parity means keeping development, staging, and production environments as similar as possible to catch issues early.
